0.title: Why Every Group Needs a Leader
0.essay:
Picture a football team where every player chases the ball, an orchestra where each musician picks his own tempo, a ship where the crew argue over every turn of the wheel, or a junction where every driver decides for himself who goes first. Without someone to lead, and others willing to follow, every human group soon falls apart.

A sad sentence

The book of Judges ends with a sentence that sums up a dark age in Israel’s history: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). Israel had forgotten its true King, the LORD, and the chapters before show plainly that when no one leads and everyone pleases himself, the weak suffer first.

A gift, not only a problem

Many of us have been hurt by leaders. But Scripture does not treat leadership as a necessary evil. Order and leadership belong to God’s good design for the world he made, and they are a kindness he shows to believers and unbelievers alike. But the answer to bad leadership is not no leadership. It is good leadership, the kind Jesus showed when he washed his friends’ feet.

Almost everyone leads somewhere, and everyone follows somewhere: at home, at work, in church and as citizens. So this study is for all of us, not only for those with a title.

Where we are going

We begin with God’s design, then ask what leadership is and how Christ turned the world’s idea of it upside down. We look at the home, the church, work and the state, and the limits God puts on every human authority. Then we turn to following well, and to practical wisdom. Other studies go deeper on parts of this, and we will point to them.

The chapters

Order by Design; What Leadership Is; Not So Among You; Leading in Every Sphere; Following Well; and In the Moment and Afterwards.

For reflection

Where do you lead, and where do you follow? Think of a group you belonged to that struggled for lack of good leadership. What was it like to be part of it?

1.title: Order by Design
1.essay:
Before there was a king, a manager or a captain, there was God, bringing order out of emptiness. Leadership is not a clever human invention for getting things done. It reflects the kind of God he is, and the kind of world he made.

A God of order

The Bible opens with a world that “was without form and void” (Genesis 1:2). Then God speaks, and everything finds its place. Even the sun and moon are given a kind of rule: “the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night” (Genesis 1:16).

When worship in Corinth became a noisy free-for-all, Paul went back to the character of God: “For God is not a God of confusion but of peace” (1 Corinthians 14:33), and so “all things should be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40). Notice the word he sets against confusion. It is not control, but peace. In Scripture the fruit of order is peace.

Made to rule under God

The first job God gave human beings was a leadership role. “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion” (Genesis 1:26). Then he blessed them: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion” (Genesis 1:28). Adam was put in the garden “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15).

This is dominion, not domination. Adam was not the owner of the garden but its keeper, a steward who makes the estate fruitful and guards it for the master’s sake. Every later form of human leadership grows from this root: a parent with a child, a farmer with a field, a manager with a team, a captain with a crew. The study Christian at Work explores what this creation calling means for our daily work.

Borrowed authority

Where does any human authority come from? Paul answers: “For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God” (Romans 13:1). Jesus said the same to the most powerful man in Jerusalem. Pilate boasted that he had authority to release him or crucify him. Jesus answered, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11).

Even a Roman governor, about to commit the worst of injustices, held his power on loan. Two things follow. First, authority is real, and those who hold it deserve respect, because God gave it. Second, authority is borrowed, and everyone who holds it will one day give account to its owner.

A common grace

Jesus said that our Father “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). Theologians call this common grace: God’s undeserved kindness to all people. It does not save anyone, but it holds back evil and lets human life flourish. Paul told a pagan crowd that God “did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons” (Acts 14:17).

Good order is one of these gifts. Honest police, a fair referee, a hospital where everyone knows their part: these bless believer and unbeliever alike. Even the traffic lights at the end of your road, which let thousands of strangers share a junction safely, are a small daily mercy from the God of order.

Why even pagans honour good leaders

Across history and across cultures, people have admired leaders who were just, brave and willing to sacrifice for others, and despised those who were cruel or greedy. Greek, Roman and Chinese writers alike praised the ruler who governed for his people’s good. This is no accident. Paul says that Gentiles who never had God’s law still “show that the work of the law is written on their hearts” (Romans 2:15). Made in the image of the perfect Ruler, people still recognise something of what a good leader looks like. Proverbs puts it simply: “When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan” (Proverbs 29:2). You do not need to be a Christian to feel the difference.

Order bent, order restored

Sin did not abolish order; it bent it. After the fall, God warned the woman that her husband “shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16), describing not his good design but the harsh rule that sin would bring. Ever since, leaders have tended to grasp and followers to rebel. Yet God did not give up on order, and he promised a King of his own. After his resurrection, Jesus said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). The rule God gave humanity at the beginning, and humanity spoiled, is held at last by a man who will never misuse it.

An example

A man who grew up with a harsh, unpredictable father learned to distrust anyone in charge. Years later he joined a volunteer lifeboat crew. One night in a heavy sea, the helmsman’s calm, clear instructions brought everyone home. Driving back at dawn, he realised that his quarrel had never really been with leadership, only with bad leadership. He went home and read Romans 13 again, slowly, for the first time without resentment.

For reflection

Where have you seen God’s common grace in good order around you this week? Do you tend to see authority as a gift or a threat, and why? How does knowing that every authority is borrowed from God change the way you see those over you? And the authority you hold?

2.title: What Leadership Is
2.essay:
We know good leadership when we see it, and feel it quickly when it is missing. But what is it? Scripture gives no textbook definition. It shows us leaders at work, good and bad, and the picture is rich and practical.

Five threads

Leadership in Scripture is woven from at least five threads.

Influence. Leading is moving others towards something good. It is not first a title. An older colleague whom everyone asks for advice may lead more than the person with the badge.

Responsibility. A leader answers for those in his care. Jesus said, “Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required” (Luke 12:48).

Direction. Someone has to say where we are going. Near the end of his life Moses prayed for a successor “who shall go out before them and come in before them, who shall lead them out and bring them in, that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep that have no shepherd” (Numbers 27:16–17).

Protection. A good leader stands between his people and harm. When enemies threatened the builders of Jerusalem’s wall, Nehemiah told them to “fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes” (Nehemiah 4:14).

Decision. In the end someone must decide. The wise leader decides after listening, and then carries the weight of it.

No one can do it alone

Exodus 18 contains one of the most practical leadership lessons in the Bible. Moses sat as judge for the whole nation “from morning till evening” (Exodus 18:13), with a queue that never shortened. His father-in-law Jethro watched and said, “What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone” (Exodus 18:17–18).

Jethro’s advice was to share the load: to teach the people God’s ways and appoint others to judge the smaller cases, so that “they will bear the burden with you” (Exodus 18:22). Good leaders raise up other leaders instead of making everyone depend on them. And good leaders listen. Moses, who had spoken with God at the burning bush, took advice from a Midianite priest: “So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said” (Exodus 18:24).

Character before charisma

What kind of people did Jethro say to choose? “Able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe” (Exodus 18:21). Ability matters. But three of the four qualities are about character. Later Moses told the tribes to choose “wise, understanding, and experienced men” (Deuteronomy 1:13), and he charged the new judges: “You shall not be partial in judgment. You shall hear the small and the great alike. You shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God’s” (Deuteronomy 1:17).

That last phrase is the heart of it. The judgment is God’s. The leader sits in God’s place for a while, so he must treat the poor and the powerful alike, and be bullied by neither. Our age is dazzled by confidence and charm. Scripture asks first: can this person be trusted with other people?

Like the morning light

David’s last words describe what a good leader is like for those under him: “When one rules justly over men, ruling in the fear of God, he dawns on them like the morning light, like the sun shining forth on a cloudless morning, like rain that makes grass to sprout from the earth” (2 Samuel 23:3–4). Good leadership is like sunrise after a long night, or rain on dry ground: things grow under it. And it rests on justice and the fear of God.

The wisdom of many voices

Proverbs returns again and again to counsel. “Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety” (Proverbs 11:14). “Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22). The opposite is a tragedy: “an old and foolish king who no longer knew how to take advice” (Ecclesiastes 4:13).

Proverbs also warns about what leaders let in. “By justice a king builds up the land, but he who exacts gifts tears it down” (Proverbs 29:4). “If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked” (Proverbs 29:12). A leader who rewards flattery will be surrounded by flatterers. One who welcomes honest bad news will hear the truth in time to act.

A gift for some, a duty for all

Paul lists leading among the gifts God gives his people: “the one who leads, with zeal” (Romans 12:8). Some are especially gifted to lead, and the church should encourage them. But everyone who carries responsibility is called to carry it faithfully, and many good leaders are quiet people who would never call themselves leaders.

An example

A newly promoted ward sister was determined to prove herself. She made every decision, checked every chart and stayed late every night. Within months she was exhausted and her team had stopped thinking for themselves. An older colleague took her aside, rather like Jethro, and told her kindly that she was going to wear herself out. She began trusting her senior nurses with more, asking their views at handover and keeping only the hardest cases for herself. The ward ran better, and so did she.

For reflection

Which of the five threads (influence, responsibility, direction, protection, decision) comes most easily to you, and which least? Where are you trying to do alone what God means to be shared? Who are your honest counsellors? Do the people around you find it easy to bring you bad news?

3.title: Not So Among You
3.essay:
Two disciples once asked Jesus for the best seats in his kingdom, and the others were furious. Jesus answered them all with words that overturned the world’s idea of leadership, and still do.

The world’s way and Christ’s way

James and John had asked, “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory” (Mark 10:37). Jesus called the twelve together and said, “You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:42–45).

Notice what Jesus does not say. He does not say that no one should lead, or that wanting to be great is always wrong. He redefines greatness. In the world, the higher you go, the more people serve you. In his kingdom, the higher you go, the more people you serve. Authority exists for the good of those under it, and its measure is the cross.

Teacher and Lord, on his knees

On the night before he died, Jesus took a towel and a basin and washed his disciples’ feet, the job of the lowest servant in the house. Then he said, “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:13–14).

He did not stop being Lord when he knelt. Servant leadership is not leadership abandoned: Jesus still taught, corrected and set the direction. But his authority came down to the floor. Paul traces the same pattern on a far larger scale: Christ Jesus, “though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). And Paul says, “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5).

Stop and wonder at this. The one who holds all authority in heaven and on earth used it to serve people who would desert him that very night. Every Christian leader is simply learning, slowly, to look a little more like him.

The shepherd-king

The Bible’s favourite picture of a leader is a shepherd. God “chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds” (Psalm 78:70), and “with upright heart he shepherded them and guided them with his skillful hand” (Psalm 78:72). A shepherd feeds, guides, protects and knows his sheep. Jesus took the picture for himself: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). The study The Lord Is My Shepherd explores this picture in depth.

When leaders fail

Scripture is honest about failed leaders, and their failures follow patterns we still see.

Fear of people. King Saul disobeyed God and then explained, “I feared the people and obeyed their voice” (1 Samuel 15:24). A leader who must be liked cannot lead.

Harshness. When Rehoboam became king, the old advisers told him, “If you will be a servant to this people today and serve them, and speak good words to them when you answer them, then they will be your servants forever” (1 Kings 12:7). He listened instead to his young friends and told the people, “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke” (1 Kings 12:14). Ten tribes walked away.

Self-feeding. Through Ezekiel God condemned Israel’s leaders: “Ah, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding yourselves! Should not shepherds feed the sheep?” (Ezekiel 34:2). They neglected the weak and the lost, “and with force and harshness you have ruled them” (Ezekiel 34:4).

Love of first place. In one early church a man named Diotrephes, “who likes to put himself first” (3 John 9), refused visitors and pushed people out.

Where a leader uses his position to frighten, control, exploit or harm, in a home, a church or a workplace, that is abuse, and it must never be covered up. Anyone being harmed should seek safety at once and report it to the authorities. A church that protects an abuser to protect its reputation has become a false shepherd itself.

Answerable to God

Every leader will give an account. Church leaders keep watch over souls “as those who will have to give an account” (Hebrews 13:17). James warns, “Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness” (James 3:1).

Yet there is hope for leaders who have failed. Peter denied Jesus three times. Jesus met him by the lake, asked him three times whether he loved him, and gave him back his work: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). Christ forgives failed leaders, and makes them gentler ones.

An example

A warehouse supervisor was known for shouting. After he became a Christian he noticed it in a new way, as a sin against the people God had put in his care. He began learning his team’s names and asking about their families. Once, after losing his temper, he apologised in front of everyone who had heard him. Several of them still mention it.

For reflection

Where do you expect to be served because of your position? Which of the four failures (fear of people, harshness, self-feeding, love of first place) is the most tempting for you? What would it mean for you to wash feet this week? How does Jesus’ restoring of Peter speak to a leader who has failed?

4.title: Leading in Every Sphere
4.essay:
God has placed authority in several different spheres of life: the home, the church, the workplace and the state. Each has its own purpose. Each is limited. And each stands under Christ, who is Lord of them all.

Different spheres, one Lord

God gives authority to different institutions for different purposes. A parent does not run the government. The government does not appoint the church’s elders. The elders do not tell you how to do your job. The Dutch theologian and statesman Abraham Kuyper called this sphere sovereignty: each sphere answers directly to God and should not swallow the others. When one does, trouble follows. This chapter gives a short survey; other studies go deeper.

The home

Ephesians 5 and 6 apply the call to submit “out of reverence for Christ” (Ephesians 5:21) to the household: wives and husbands, children and parents. Husbands are told, “love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), and fathers, “do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). Christians differ on what this means for husbands and wives. Complementarians hold that husbands are given a real responsibility to lead; egalitarians, out of love for Scripture and a right concern that women never be belittled, read these verses as mutual submission without distinct roles.

This commentary’s view: the complementarian reading, held gently. Husband and wife are equal in worth and different by design, and headship is exercised only as Christ exercises it, in self-giving love, never by domination. The studies Christian Marriage, Biblical Manhood and Christian Parenting set this out fully.

The church

Christ alone is head of the church. Under him, each local church is led by a plurality of qualified elders, with deacons serving and the congregation involved in key decisions. Peter writes, “shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly” (1 Peter 5:2), and “not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3). Paul says, “If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task” (1 Timothy 3:1), and then lists mostly character, not skills. Its power is the word of God and a life worth following, never force. The study The Church covers elders and deacons in its chapter “Shepherds and Servants”.

Work

Paul spoke to slaves and masters, in a world where slavery was very different from modern employment and was never grounded in creation. Yet his principles carry over to every workplace. Workers serve “with a good will as to the Lord and not to man” (Ephesians 6:7). Masters must “stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him” (Ephesians 6:9). “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1). The studies Leading a Business for Christ and Christian at Work work this out in detail.

The state

Government is “God’s servant for your good” (Romans 13:4), given to punish wrongdoing and protect the innocent. Christians are to “be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution” (1 Peter 2:13), to pay their taxes, to show respect, and to pray “for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life” (1 Timothy 2:2). Exiles in Babylon were told, “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). The study The Christian & the World treats government at length.

Where every authority stops

Every human authority is real, but none is absolute. When the council ordered the apostles to stop preaching, Peter and John replied, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge” (Acts 4:19), and later, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego told the king that God could rescue them from the furnace, “But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (Daniel 3:18). When prayer was banned, Daniel went home and prayed, “as he had done previously” (Daniel 6:10).

Notice the pattern. They refused only what would have meant sinning. They refused openly, not by trickery. They stayed respectful and accepted the consequences. This commentary holds that Christians should submit in all lawful things, even to unjust rulers, and refuse only where obeying would mean disobeying God. Disliking a decision is not the same as being commanded to sin.

Abuse is never permitted

No human authority, in any sphere, has the right to abuse. Not headship, not eldership, not an employer, not the state. Where there is abuse, safety comes first. Get to a safe place, tell someone you trust, and report it to the police or the proper authorities. Leaving to escape abuse is not rebellion against God’s order. And Christians are called to “open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute” (Proverbs 31:8), speaking up for those who cannot.

An example

An administrator in a hospital was asked by her manager to adjust the waiting-list figures before an inspection. She worked hard for him, but she quietly said she could not do it, explained why, and offered to help prepare an honest account of the delays instead. He was angry for a week. She kept working well and spoke respectfully of him. Months later he thanked her.

For reflection

In which spheres do you hold authority, and in which are you under it? Have you seen one sphere overreach into another? How do the apostles and Daniel show the difference between disobedience and faithful refusal? If you or someone you know is being harmed by a person in authority, who could you tell this week?

5.title: Following Well
5.essay:
Most of us spend far more of life following than leading. Scripture has a great deal to say about following, and none of it is servile. Good following is an act of faith and a gift to the group.

Submission without servility

Paul sums up the Spirit-filled life with the words “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ” (Ephesians 5:21). The word for submitting was originally a military word: to arrange under, to take your ordered place in the ranks.

As this commentary explains on that verse, two things must be held together. First, submission says nothing about worth. The Son is equal with the Father in being, power and glory, yet in the work of salvation he willingly came as the one the Father sent and obeyed him even to death. Order and equality are not rivals. Second, submission is voluntary. It is something a person gives; nobody can submit someone else, and no one in the passage is told to make others submit. A leader who sets out to force submission has shown that what he really wants is control.

And it is done “out of reverence for Christ”. That phrase is both the engine and the limit. You do not follow because the other person has earned it, but before the face of the Lord who gave everything for you. And because the reverence is for Christ, it can never require what Christ forbids. Verse 21 sets the humble, other-centred spirit in which all Christians relate; the verses that follow then show the particular order God has given in the home and at work, where some lead and others follow, and both serve.

Honour

Peter sums up our duties in four short commands: “Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor” (1 Peter 2:17). The emperor was Nero. Paul asks believers to esteem their church leaders “very highly in love because of their work” (1 Thessalonians 5:13).

Honour is shown in small things: how we speak about a boss when he is not in the room, and what we post about a politician. David had every reason to hate King Saul, who was trying to kill him. Yet when he had the chance to strike, he refused, because Saul was “the LORD’s anointed” (1 Samuel 24:6).

Prayer

“First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:1–2). It is hard to despise someone you pray for by name. Pray for your manager, your pastor, your head teacher and your prime minister, including the ones you did not choose.

Followers who make leaders better

Hebrews tells believers to obey and submit to their leaders, and adds, “Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you” (Hebrews 13:17). Followers shape leaders. A grumbling team makes even a good leader worse; an honest, willing one makes an ordinary leader better.

When Moses grew tired during a battle, “Aaron and Hur held up his hands” (Exodus 17:12). That is what good followers do. They tell the truth early, and bring solutions, not only complaints. They encourage, which leaders need more than they admit.

Respectful disagreement

Following is not silence. Nathan confronted King David. Abigail stopped David from a terrible act of revenge, and he thanked God for her “discretion” (1 Samuel 25:33). Paul says of Peter, “I opposed him to his face” (Galatians 2:11).

But how we disagree matters. Speak privately first where you can. Speak respectfully, with facts rather than rumours. Remember the call “to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people” (Titus 3:2). Then, unless what is decided is sin, accept the decision and support it with a good heart. You have done your part, and God can look after the outcome.

When leaders fail

It helps to tell apart the weak, the wrong and the wicked. A weak leader needs patience, prayer and help. A leader who makes a wrong decision needs honest, respectful counsel, and then, unless the decision requires sin, loyal support. A leader who is wicked, who lies, exploits or abuses, must not be obeyed in the wrong, and must be reported. In a church, serious charges against an elder go to the other elders with proper evidence (1 Timothy 5:19), and crimes go to the police. Abuse is never something to quietly put up with. Safety comes first.

And behind every failed leader stands the one who never fails. When Jesus saw the crowds, “he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36). He is that shepherd. However poorly we are led on earth, we are never unled.

An example

A church member was upset by the elders’ decision to change the time of the evening service. She wrote a long, sharp email, then deleted it and asked to meet one of them instead. She listened to their reasons and said honestly why she still disagreed. The decision stood. She chose to support it, and a year later she was asked to help lead the new evening group.

For reflection

Do you find it harder to honour leaders you dislike, or to disagree with leaders you like? Who are you praying for by name? What could you do this month to make a leader’s work a joy rather than a groan? When a leader has let you down, which was it: weak, wrong or wicked?

6.title: In the Moment and Afterwards
6.essay:
Ideas about leadership are easy; Monday morning is hard. This chapter gathers practical wisdom for the moments when you have to lead or follow, and for the evenings afterwards, when you go over how it went.

At home

Leadership at home is mostly small and repeated: praying with your family, setting the tone in a tense moment, being the first to apologise, taking the lead on hard conversations instead of letting them drift. Following at home is the same: supporting a decision once your voice has been heard, and refusing to undermine each other in front of the children. Both are done under Christ, who loves the family more than either of you.

At work

If you lead a team, learn their names, their strengths and their burdens. “Know well the condition of your flocks” (Proverbs 27:23). Praise in public and correct in private. Give credit away and take blame on yourself. If you are led, work “heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23), whether or not anyone notices.

At church, on a team and in the community

Many people lead without pay or title: running a children’s group, coaching an under-tens side, organising a rota. Do it as service, not as a platform. Turn up, keep your word, and look out for the person on the edge. And if it is your turn to follow, be the volunteer every organiser hopes for.

Humility and listening

“Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger” (James 1:19). “If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (Proverbs 18:13). Before a decision, ask who you have not heard yet, and who it will affect most.

Taking responsibility

Adam blamed Eve, and Eve blamed the serpent. Good leaders break that chain. When something goes wrong on your watch, say so plainly: this was my decision, and I got it wrong. “Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). Few things build trust faster than a leader who owns his mistakes.

Making decisions

Pray. Gather the facts. Seek counsel, because “in an abundance of counselors there is safety” (Proverbs 11:14). Ask what is right before asking what is easy. Then decide, explain your reasons, and carry the cost. A leader who waits until he is certain will usually wait too long.

When there is conflict

Every group that does anything together will have disagreements. Deal with them early, directly and gently: “If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone” (Matthew 18:15). Do not let a quarrel fester because you dread the conversation. The study Handling Conflict gives detailed help for the hard conversation itself.

Using influence for others

Whatever influence you have, a vote, a budget, a seat at the table, a following online, is a trust. “Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others” (Philippians 2:4). Use it to open doors for those who have none and to speak for those not in the room.

The fear of man in leaders

Many leaders fail not from cruelty but from fear: fear of being disliked, of a hard meeting, of losing a vote. Saul obeyed the people instead of God. Paul asked, “Am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God?” (Galatians 1:10). “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). A leader secure in God’s verdict can make the unpopular right decision, and can also admit he was wrong. The study The Fear of Man explores this freedom.

Afterwards

When the day is over and you replay a meeting or an argument, bring it to God honestly. Thank him for what went well. Confess what was sinful, and put right what you can. Leave the rest with him. You are not the world’s saviour, or even your team’s. You are a steward, and “it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2), not that they be perfect.

The King whose government has no end

All our leading and following is temporary. Prime ministers leave office, managers retire, elders grow old, and parents let their children go. But Isaiah saw a child born for us on whose shoulder the government would rest: “his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end” (Isaiah 9:6–7).

That is Jesus. He is the leader every group on earth has been longing for: perfectly just, endlessly patient, wiser than every counsellor, strong enough to protect, and humble enough to wash feet. Until he comes again, we lead and follow as his servants, in his name, imperfect echoes of the King whose kingdom will never fail.

An example

A head teacher in his last year before retirement was asked what he had learned about leadership. He said that early on he thought it meant having all the answers, and later getting people to like him. Near the end he saw that it meant serving the children, telling the truth to the staff and trusting God with what he could not control. He kept a card on his desk with Mark 10:45 on it, and he left it there for the next head.

For reflection

Which one of these practical habits do you most need to begin this week? Where is the fear of man shaping your leading or following? What mistake might you need to own? How does knowing that Christ’s government will have no end give you peace about the leaders you have now, and about your own failures?
